stem: What is the approximate resting potential of a mammalian neurone?

options.content: −70 mV
options.rationale: Correct: the inside is about 70 mV negative to the outside.

options.content: +40 mV
options.rationale: This is close to the peak of an action potential.
Far more negative than a typical resting potential.

options.content: 0 mV
options.rationale: At 0 mV the membrane would not be polarised at all.

explanation: The resting potential is about **−70 mV** (inside negative).

stem: During the depolarisation phase of an action potential, which ions move, and in which direction?

options.content: Sodium ions diffuse into the axon
options.rationale: Correct: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

options.content: Potassium ions diffuse out of the axon
options.rationale: That is repolarisation.

options.content: Sodium ions are pumped out of the axon
options.rationale: Pumping Na⁺ out maintains the resting potential.

options.content: Potassium ions are pumped into the axon
options.rationale: The pump does this all the time; it does not depolarise.

explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ diffuses **in**, making the inside positive.

stem: For each molecule of ATP hydrolysed, the sodium-potassium pump moves

options.content: 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: 2 Na⁺ out of the cell and 3 K⁺ into the cell
options.rationale: The numbers are reversed.

options.content: 3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out of the cell
options.rationale: The directions are reversed.

options.content: 1 Na⁺ out of the cell and 1 K⁺ into the cell
options.rationale: The pump is not a one-for-one exchanger.

explanation: Three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, so more positive charge leaves than enters.

stem: Why is the inside of a resting axon negative relative to the outside?

options.content: The membrane is more permeable to Na⁺, which diffuses in
options.rationale: Na⁺ entry would make the inside positive.

options.content: Voltage-gated sodium channels are open at rest
options.rationale: They are closed at rest.

options.content: The membrane is more permeable to K⁺, which diffuses out
options.rationale: Correct: open K⁺ channels let K⁺ leave, together with the pump.

options.content: Chloride ions are pumped in by the sodium-potassium pump
options.rationale: The pump moves Na⁺ and K⁺ only.

explanation: At rest some K⁺ channels are open, so the membrane is more permeable to K⁺, which diffuses out down its concentration gradient; the pump also moves more positive charge out than in.

stem: A sensory receptor is described as a transducer because it

options.content: amplifies an action potential so it can reach the brain
options.rationale: Action potentials are not amplified; they are all-or-nothing.

options.content: transmits impulses from one neurone to another across a gap
options.rationale: That is a synapse.

options.content: stores neurotransmitter until a strong stimulus arrives
options.rationale: This is not the meaning of transducer.

options.content: converts the energy of a stimulus into an electrical change
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A transducer converts one form of energy (light, chemical, pressure) into another: an electrical receptor potential.

stem: Stimuli of increasing strength are applied to a sensory neurone, all above threshold. What happens to the action potentials recorded?

options.content: Their size increases but their frequency stays the same
options.rationale: Action potentials are all the same size.

options.content: Both their size and their frequency increase
options.rationale: Size is fixed by the all-or-nothing principle.

options.content: Neither changes, because the threshold has been reached
options.rationale: Frequency does change with stimulus strength.

options.content: Their frequency increases but their size stays the same
options.rationale: Correct: all-or-nothing; strength is coded by frequency.

explanation: Above threshold, action potentials are always the same size; a stronger stimulus increases their frequency.

stem: In a taste-bud chemoreceptor, what is the immediate effect of sodium ions from food entering the receptor cell?

options.content: An action potential is produced at once in the receptor cell itself
options.rationale: The receptor cell gives a graded receptor potential first.

options.content: The receptor cell hyperpolarises and releases transmitter
options.rationale: Entry of positive ions depolarises, not hyperpolarises.

options.content: The receptor cell depolarises, producing a receptor potential
options.rationale: Correct: a graded depolarisation.

options.content: Potassium channels open and the cell returns to rest
options.rationale: This is not the first effect of Na⁺ entry.

explanation: Na⁺ entry makes the inside less negative: a receptor potential, which leads to transmitter release onto a sensory neurone.
hints: Positive ions entering a cell have what effect on the potential?

stem: A drug blocks voltage-gated potassium channels but has no effect on other channels or on the pump. Which change to the action potential is most likely?

options.content: Depolarisation is prevented, so no action potential can occur at all
options.rationale: Sodium channels still open, so depolarisation still happens.

options.content: Repolarisation is slowed, so the action potential lasts longer
options.rationale: Correct: K⁺ cannot leave quickly through voltage-gated channels.

options.content: The peak potential falls to about −50 mV
options.rationale: The peak depends on Na⁺ entry, which is not blocked.

options.content: Hyperpolarisation becomes larger than usual
options.rationale: Hyperpolarisation is caused by K⁺ channels staying open, so it would be reduced.

explanation: Without voltage-gated K⁺ channels, K⁺ can leave only through the leak channels, so repolarisation is slow and hyperpolarisation small or absent.
hints: Which phase depends on voltage-gated potassium channels?

stem: Sodium ions enter an axon during an action potential by active transport.
explanation: False. Na⁺ enters by facilitated diffusion through voltage-gated sodium channels, down its electrochemical gradient.

stem: A stimulus that does not reach the threshold produces no action potential.
explanation: True: the all-or-nothing principle.

stem: Match each phase of the action potential with the event that causes it.

right.content: K⁺ channels are slow to close, so too much K⁺ leaves
Sodium-potassium pump and K⁺ leak channels
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ diffuses out

explanation: Na⁺ in (depolarisation), K⁺ out (repolarisation), K⁺ overshoot (hyperpolarisation), pump and leak (resting).

stem: Choose the correct words.

payload.template: When the membrane reaches the {{blank:a}}, voltage-gated {{blank:b}} channels open. For a short time afterwards no new action potential can be produced; this is the {{blank:c}} period.

explanation: Threshold → sodium channels open; afterwards the refractory period.

stem: Name the principle that states that an action potential either occurs at full size or does not occur at all.
explanation: The **all-or-nothing** principle.

stem: A trace shows a resting potential of -72 mV and an action potential peak of +40 mV. Calculate the total change in potential from rest to peak, in mV.
explanation: 40 − (-72) = **112 mV**. Ignoring the sign of the resting potential gives 40 mV, which is wrong.
workedSolution: 1. 40 − (-72) = **112 mV**. Ignoring the sign of the resting potential gives 40 mV, which is wrong.

stem: The absolute refractory period of a neurone is 2.5 ms. Calculate the maximum number of action potentials per second that this neurone could carry.
explanation:
1. Shortest interval between action potentials $= 2.5\ \text{ms} = 0.0025\ \text{s}$.
2. Maximum frequency $= \dfrac{1}{0.0025} = 400$ per second.
Dividing 1 by 2.5 without converting to seconds gives 0.4, which is wrong.
workedSolution:
1. Shortest interval between action potentials $= 2.5\ \text{ms} = 0.0025\ \text{s}$.
2. Maximum frequency $= \dfrac{1}{0.0025} = 400$ per second.
Dividing 1 by 2.5 without converting to seconds gives 0.4, which is wrong.

stem: Explain how the resting potential of an axon is established and maintained.

points.description: Sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
This sets up concentration gradients: more Na⁺ outside, more K⁺ inside
Membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ (some K⁺ channels open, Na⁺ channels closed), so K⁺ diffuses out
Leaving the inside negative (about −70 mV) / large negative ions such as proteins stay inside

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move three sodium ions out of the axon for every two potassium ions in, setting up concentration gradients with more Na⁺ outside and more K⁺ inside. At rest the membrane is much more permeable to K⁺ because some potassium channels are open while sodium channels are closed, so K⁺ diffuses out down its gradient. Large negatively charged proteins remain inside, so the inside is left about 70 mV negative to the outside.

explanation: Pump, gradients, differential permeability, result.
hints: Give both the pump and the permeability.

stem: Describe how a chemoreceptor cell in a taste bud responds to salt and leads to impulses in a sensory neurone.

points.description: Na⁺ diffuse into the receptor cell through channels (in the microvilli)
Depolarising the receptor cell / producing a receptor potential, which is graded
Ca²⁺ channels open and neurotransmitter is released onto the sensory neurone; if the generator potential reaches threshold, an action potential is produced

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sodium ions from the salt diffuse into the receptor cell through channels in its microvilli, depolarising it and producing a graded receptor potential. This opens voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium ions enter and the cell releases neurotransmitter onto a sensory neurone. If the resulting generator potential reaches the threshold, an action potential is set up in the sensory neurone.

explanation: Na⁺ entry, receptor potential, transmitter release, threshold.
hints: Start with the ion that enters.

stem: Suggest why a person poisoned with a substance that inhibits ATP synthesis eventually loses the ability to produce action potentials.

points.description: The sodium-potassium pump needs ATP / stops working
Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients run down / are no longer maintained
So the resting potential is lost and Na⁺ cannot diffuse in rapidly enough to depolarise the membrane / no action potential

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The sodium-potassium pump needs ATP, so it stops. Na⁺ leaks in and K⁺ leaks out until the concentration gradients run down. The resting potential is then lost, and there is no steep sodium gradient to drive the rapid entry of Na⁺, so action potentials can no longer be produced. This takes time because each action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the ions.

explanation: Link ATP → pump → gradients → no action potential.
hints: Which process at rest needs ATP?

parts.stem: At which time were voltage-gated potassium channels most likely to be open while sodium channels were closed?

options.content: 0.6 ms

options.content: 1.2 ms
options.rationale: Correct: the potential is falling from the peak (repolarisation).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the change in potential between 0.6 ms and 0.9 ms.

points.description: Threshold has been reached (about −50 mV at 0.6 ms)
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (many, by positive feedback)
Na⁺ diffuse in, so the inside becomes positive, reaching +38 mV

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: By 0.6 ms the membrane had reached the threshold of about −50 mV, so many voltage-gated sodium channels opened. Sodium ions diffused in down their electrochemical gradient, making the inside positive and raising the potential to +38 mV at 0.9 ms.

stem: An axon was stimulated with single stimuli of increasing strength. Responses were recorded as follows: stimulus 1 gave a small change of 6 mV that died away; stimulus 2 gave a change of 12 mV that died away; stimulus 3 and stimulus 4 each gave an action potential reaching +35 mV.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the potential that must be reached for an action potential to occur.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why stimuli 1 and 2 did not produce action potentials.

points.description: The depolarisation did not reach the threshold
Not enough voltage-gated Na⁺ channels opened to start positive feedback / all-or-nothing

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stimuli 1 and 2 depolarised the membrane by only 6 and 12 mV, so it did not reach the threshold; too few voltage-gated sodium channels opened for the rapid influx of Na⁺ that produces an action potential.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Stimulus 4 was stronger than stimulus 3. Explain why the action potentials were the same size.

points.description: All-or-nothing principle: once threshold is reached a full action potential occurs
The size depends on the Na⁺ gradient / Na⁺ channels, not on stimulus strength

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Action potentials are all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, the voltage-gated sodium channels open fully and the potential rises to the same peak, set by the sodium gradient, whatever the stimulus strength.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest how a sensory neurone would signal that a stimulus was stronger.

points.description: By a higher frequency of action potentials

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It would produce action potentials more frequently.

explanation: Threshold, all-or-nothing, frequency coding.
hints: Compare the sub-threshold and full responses.
